audits.question: Check mlqrt/Melqart's king-of-the-city analysis and the limits of a fixed merchant-patron/theological profile against an inscription, philological source or scholarly passage.
audits.entry_locator: §4 bullet 1 (line 76) is the tested claim; related anchors: §3 Melqart table row (line 64), §4 Arados AO 7676 bullet (line 80), §4 Briquel-Chatonnet bullet (line 82), §4 Josephus/Menander bullet (line 83)
audits.entry_claim: Line 76: "The name *mlqrt*, conventionally Melqart, is understood as 'king of the city'; its civic semantics are more productive than assigning the god the modern job 'patron of merchants' alone (Bonnet 1988)." Related bounded rows: line 64 licenses "city kingship, homeland ties, and translated cult identities" and forbids flattening to "simply Heracles with a different name"; line 82: bilingual versions "can differ in audience, identity claims, and formulation".
audits.source_citation: Wikipedia (English, current revision as extracted 2026-10-17), "Melqart" — tertiary article relaying Lipiński, Edward (2002), Semitic Languages: Outline of a Comparative Grammar, Orientalia Lovaniensia Analecta 80, Peeters, p. 235, and relaying Aubet, María Eugenia (2001), The Phoenicians and the West, 2nd ed.
audits.source_locator: Article sections as extracted: opening definition; paragraph beginning "Melqart was written in the Phoenician abjad as MLQRT"; "Archaeological evidence" section (Aubet relay); "Attempts at a synthesis" section (Albright/underworld debate)
audits.source_excerpt: Edward Lipinski theorizes that it was derived from MLK QRT (Mīlk-Qārt), which means "King of the City".
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL direct public web retrieval of the live article page (same batch as Louvre/Persée/PLOS fetches, 2026-10-17 ~17:40–17:44 UTC); no login, no API
audits.basis: The retrieved page gives the philological derivation the entry asserts (mlqrt as MLK QRT "king of the city", attributed to Lipiński 2002 p. 235), confirms the civic/tutelary framing ("tutelary god of the Phoenician city-state of Tyre"), documents a merchant-protector function as one attested role among others (Aubet relay: temple in each new colony, god "invoked in oaths sanctioning contracts"), and shows the theological profile is live and unfixed ("The paucity of evidence on Melqart has led to debate as to the nature of his cult"; Albright's underworld "King of the City" alternative, with others calling it coincidental and "the city in question could conceivably be Tyre"). All of this matches the entry's calibration: the civic reading is productive; a fixed merchant job description is not warranted; the god is not "simply Heracles with a different name" (Greek identification is an equivalence act, see corroborations). Scope is partial because the etymology arrives through a tertiary relay — Lipiński 2002 p. 235 itself was not opened — and the entry's named Bonnet (1988) analysis was not directly inspected.
audits.coupling_implication: The entry's civic-cult-network coupling stays licensed but must remain multi-role: contract-oath guarantor, colonial temple founder, royal/high-priestly Tyrian cult, debated underworld aspect, and Hellenistic gymnasium dedicatee can coexist on one divine name. Design systems should attach functions to dated localities and institutions, never to a single modern occupational profile; equivalence tables with Greek gods are diplomatic instruments, not biography transfers.
audits.limits: Tertiary mediator: the Lipiński derivation is quoted from Wikipedia with its page citation, not from the Peeters grammar itself; Wikipedia also carries unsourced or citation-needed passages (excluded from this basis). Bonnet 1988 — the entry's cited authority — remains unread; a printed-library check would upgrade scope beyond partial. Live attempts at stronger sources failed and were recorded, not ground further: melqart.huma-num.fr (Bonnet team's Melqart repertory) did not resolve (DNS ENOTFOUND), and livius.org/articles/religion/melqart/ returned HTTP 404; web search quota was exhausted, so no alternate philological source was located this session. Language/edition actually inspected: English Wikipedia revision of 2026-10-17; Lipiński's original English text unread.

corroboration.label: inscription / museum object: Louvre AO 7676 (Arados bilingual statue base)
corroboration.source_citation: Musée du Louvre, Département des Antiquités orientales, object record AO 7676, "base de statue", Hellenistic −25/−24, found at Arados (Arwad); record last updated 16.06.2025
corroboration.source_locator: Description/Features and Inscriptions fields of the collections record
corroboration.source_excerpt: Inscription bilingue grecque (3 lignes) et phénicienne (3 lignes) : dédicace aux dieux du gymnase, Hermès et Héraclès-Milqart
corroboration.note: French museum record inspected. Confirms the entry's line 80 exactly: a very late (−25/−24) bilingual pairing Greek Heracles with Phoenician Milqart among the gods of a gymnasium — 'translated cult identity' attested on an inscription, in an institutional setting the entry correctly refuses to project back onto Bronze Age Tyre. The record also cites Bonnet 1988 p. 117 and Briquel-Chatonnet 1991/2012/2019 for this object.

corroboration.source_citation: Briquel-Chatonnet, Françoise (2012), "Les inscriptions phénico-grecques et le bilinguisme des Phéniciens", Comptes rendus des séances de l'Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres 156(1): 619–638
corroboration.source_locator: Opening communication paragraphs, p. 619 (French original as extracted)
corroboration.source_excerpt: celles-ci ne sont pas toujours équivalentes, car elles ne s'adressent pas au même public et qu'il y a toujours une langue de base, dans laquelle le texte a été pensé et élaboré, avant d'être traduit

Directly supports entry line 82: bilingual versions are not always equivalent, address different publics, and have a base language; the same opening singles out "la bilingue d'Arados" as "totalement original" within the corpus — consistent with the entry's use of AO 7676 as a special late case.

corroboration.source_citation: Herodotus, Histories 2.44 (English translation reproduced in the Wikipedia article) and Josephus, Against Apion 1.18 / Antiquities 8.5.3 citing Menander of Ephesus (Whiston translation, reproduced in the same page)
corroboration.source_locator: Sections quoting Herodotus 2.44 and Josephus/Menander on Hiram's egersis
corroboration.source_excerpt: They said that the temple was built at the same time that the city was founded, and that the foundation of the city took place 2,300 years ago.
corroboration.note: Ancient texts read only as English translations embedded in the tertiary page (mediator: Wikipedia; Greek/Latin originals not collated). Matches entry line 78: priests' antiquity claim reported by Greek inquiry, and line 83: egersis/Peritius festival at second hand — transmitted reportage, not a Phoenician chronicle.

audits.open_questions: 1) Parent/library: open Lipiński 2002, p. 235 (or Bonnet 1988) to upgrade the etymology from tertiary relay to direct philological inspection. 2) Is the Bonnet-team Melqart repertory (melqart.huma-num.fr) permanently moved — worth re-checking the hostname next round rather than treating the DNS failure as a source verdict. 3) The entry's mlqrt reading treats 'king of the city' as conventional understanding; Albright's Milku/Nergal 'king of the (under)city' alternative noted in the tertiary page is one more reason the entry's hedged wording should never be tightened.

audits.question: Check the entry's purple-dye production/elite display coupling using actual archaeological or technical evidence; distinguish a dye workshop/object from a universal king-only wearing law and native garment term.
audits.entry_locator: §7 bullets (lines 120–124) are the tested claim cluster; related anchors: §5 Purple textile table row (line 95), §7 everyday-dress to-verify (line 130), §7 sumptuary caution (line 135)
audits.entry_claim: Lines 123–124 (bounded compound assertion): "Timna's late-eleventh/early-tenth-century BCE wool fibers provide direct chemical evidence of shellfish purple far inland. They demonstrate consumption and connectivity, not that the wearers were Phoenicians; proposed coastal production origins remain inference. Purple technology predates Iron Age Phoenician expansion and occurred beyond Phoenician communities. A Phoenician monopoly on its invention or use is unsupported (Sukenik et al. 2021)."
audits.source_citation: Sukenik N, Iluz D, Amar Z, Varvak A, Shamir O, Ben-Yosef E (2021), "Early evidence of royal purple dyed textile from Timna Valley (Israel)", PLoS ONE 16(1): e0245897 (open access, peer-reviewed; full English text as published)
audits.source_locator: Abstract; Introduction, paragraph on the early history of purple dyeing (shell heaps, Santorini/Rhodes pigments, Nuzi and Amarna texts, Knossos 'royal purple' tablet, argaman/tekhelet); Discussion, paragraph beginning "According to our results the dyeing process of all samples was based on..." and paragraph beginning "It is reasonable to suggest that the Timna samples..."
audits.source_excerpt: The samples originated from excavations at the extensive Iron Age copper smelting site of "Slaves' Hill" (Site 34), which is tightly dated by radiocarbon to the late 11th–early 10th centuries BCE.
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL direct public web retrieval of the open-access full-text HTML (article is CC-BY); quotations copied from the published English text
audits.basis: Every sentence of the bounded claim is evidenced by retrieved article text. (1) Direct chemical evidence, inland, dated: HPLC-detected 6-monobromoindigotin/6,6-dibromoindigotin is "unequivocal evidence for the use of murex-derived purple dyestuff", on prestigious wool from Slaves' Hill (Site 34), "tightly dated by radiocarbon to the late 11th–early 10th centuries BCE" — the Arabah, not the coast. (2) Consumption/connectivity, not Phoenician wearers: the fibers sit in the assemblage of the "nomadic society operating the mines (early Edom)", and the paper itself notes the three murex species "are present in the Mediterranean Sea and are not found in the Red Sea" (transport into the interior); coastal production is framed as inference — "It is reasonable to suggest that the Timna samples are a product of the dyeing industry in the Phoenician Coastal Plain". (3) Predates Phoenician expansion / beyond Phoenician communities: shell-heap dyeing evidence "dated to around the 19th century BCE... associated with the Minoans", "a multiregional origin of the purple dyeing industry, including regions outside the Aegean", murex pigments in 17th-century-BCE wall paintings, Nuzi (1425 BCE) and Amarna (14th c. BCE) textual references — all before and beyond Iron Age Phoenician settlement. (4) No monopoly asserted anywhere in the paper; elite/royal couplings are carried by external textual traditions (biblical argaman/tekhelet for "people of the highest social rank"; Classical authors), which is evidence of prestige value, not of a Phoenician statute.
audits.coupling_implication: The production/display coupling decomposes exactly as the entry requires: a dye workshop or dyed object (Timna fragments; proposed coastal workshop sites Tyre, Shikmona, Kabri) proves chemistry, cost and connectivity; it does not identify the wearer's ethnicity, rank law, or garment vocabulary. Fiction systems should grade display by amount, shade, quality and occasion (entry §7 menu) and treat any wearing restriction as a separate, separately-evidenced institution — and keep a native garment term unattested rather than borrowing 'Tyrian purple' as a native word.
audits.limits: The 'universal king-only wearing law' part of the question is verified only as calibrated absence: the article contains no Phoenician sumptuary evidence at all (its elite references are biblical and Classical textual traditions), and the entry itself keeps line 135 as not-established (to-verify) — absence of evidence here is region- and genre-biased, not a proof that no restriction existed. The 'native garment term' half of the question (entry line 130 to-verify) is untouched by this source and stays open. Species attribution is paper-cautioned: B. brandaris or S. haemastoma indistinguishable in two samples, H. trunculus double-dyeing 'most probably' in one — matching the entry's own line 122 caution; Pliny's two-bath reading is ancient technical text in English translation, not a collated edition. The paper's Timna radiocarbon range (~1021–955 BCE window reported in the paper's body) supports the entry's 'late-eleventh/early-tenth-century' phrasing; precise boundary dates remain radiocarbon-calibrated estimates. Language/edition actually inspected: PLOS ONE full-text HTML, English, published 2021-01-28; no paywall or bot wall was hit.

corroboration.label: predates/beyond-Phoenician evidence paragraph
corroboration.source_excerpt: the first archaeological evidence that regards the purple dyeing industry are indirect evidence which includes heaps of murex shells, that are dated to around the 19th century BCE. In most cases, this early evidence is associated with the Minoans
corroboration.note: Same retrieved text continues: 'recent archaeomalacological analyses raised the possibility of a multiregional origin of the purple dyeing industry, including regions outside the Aegean'.

corroboration.label: coastal production origin is inference, not finding
corroboration.source_locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning "It is reasonable to suggest..."
corroboration.source_excerpt: It is reasonable to suggest that the Timna samples are a product of the dyeing industry in the Phoenician Coastal Plain.
corroboration.note: Hedged probabilistic wording ('It is reasonable to suggest') matches the entry's 'proposed coastal production origins remain inference' (line 123); the same paragraph locates the Iron-Age purple-industry concentration on the northern coast (Tyre, Shikmona, Kabri, Keisen).

corroboration.label: inland transport = connectivity claim
corroboration.source_excerpt: The three murex species discussed above are present in the Mediterranean Sea and are not found in the Red Sea
corroboration.note: Underwrites 'far inland' + 'connectivity' (line 123): the dye stuff reached the Arabah from the Mediterranean coast or via trade, and the wearers are the mining-site population, not identifiable Phoenicians.

corroboration.label: elite display rests on textual prestige traditions, not a Phoenician statute
corroboration.source_locator: Introduction, paragraph on argaman/tekhelet and Classical sources
corroboration.source_excerpt: It also indicates that purple textiles were highly valued and served as a symbol of prestige, social status and power.
corroboration.note: Same paragraph: biblical argaman/tekhelet are 'mentioned in the Hebrew Bible in relation to clothing of people of the highest social rank (for example, the garments of the High Priest, Exodus 28:6, and the Midianite kings, Judges 8:26)' and 'Most of the textual evidence relating to royal purple comes from the Classical era' — i.e., the royal/elite register is carried by Hebrew-bible and Graeco-Roman texts, precisely the external-tradition distinction the entry draws at lines 99 and 135.

audits.open_questions: 1) Native Phoenician/Punic garment vocabulary (entry line 130 to-verify): no epigraphic garment-term passage was located this session; parent may queue KAI/Gibson-driven term check (e.g., any attested word for dyed cloth) as a future bounded audit. 2) A positive 'workshop' object for audit contrast: the paper names coastal candidate sites (Tyre, Shikmona, Tel Kabri, Tel Keisen) from prior literature — a future audit could inspect one Shikmona excavation report directly instead of citing it through this paper. 3) Timna radiocarbon boundary dates are calibrated estimates; any future entry tightening of 'late-eleventh/early-tenth' should re-check the paper's Table 1 ranges.
